---
title: "Agriculture, Food, and Land Use（农业、食物与土地使用）"
---

## Land, Water, and Agricultural Production（土地、水与农业生产）

Agriculture（农业）is the practice of cultivating land, growing crops, and raising animals for food, fibre（纤维）, fuel（燃料）, and other products essential to human civilisation. Agriculture allowed humans to transition from nomadic hunter-gatherer lifestyles（游牧的狩猎采集生活方式）to settled communities（定居社区）, producing food surpluses（食物剩余）that supported population growth, specialisation of labour（劳动分工）, and the development of cities, writing, and complex societies. Today, agriculture occupies approximately 40 percent of the Earth's ice-free land surface（无冰地表）and employs more than one billion people worldwide, making it the single largest human use of land and the foundation of global food security（全球粮食安全的基础）.

Agricultural production depends on two fundamental resources: land and water. Land（土地）provides the physical space, soil structure（土壤结构）, and nutrients（养分）that crops need to grow. The availability of land suitable for agriculture（适合农业的土地）is limited — only about 11 percent of the Earth's land surface has soil and climate conditions suitable for crop production without major modification. The rest is too dry（过于干旱）, too cold（过于寒冷）, too steep（过于陡峭）, too rocky（岩石过多）, or has soil too poor in nutrients to support cultivation. As the global population grows and urbanisation consumes agricultural land（城市化占用农业用地）, the amount of arable land per person（人均可耕地）decreases continuously. Farmers must produce more food from the same or diminishing land area — a challenge that requires increasing productivity（提高生产率）while protecting the natural resources that production depends on.

Water（水）is essential for plant growth — plants use water for photosynthesis（光合作用）, nutrient transport（养分运输）, cell expansion（细胞膨胀）, and temperature regulation through transpiration（蒸腾作用）. Without adequate water, crops cannot grow regardless of soil fertility（土壤肥力）or other inputs. Water for agriculture comes from two main sources that define different farming systems（农业系统）. Rain-fed agriculture（雨养农业）depends entirely on rainfall（降雨）and is the most common form of agriculture worldwide, covering approximately 80 percent of cultivated land. Rain-fed systems are vulnerable to drought（干旱）and changing rainfall patterns（降雨模式变化）, which can cause crop failure（作物歉收）and food insecurity（粮食不安全）. Irrigated agriculture（灌溉农业）supplements or replaces rainfall with water from rivers（河流）, lakes（湖泊）, reservoirs（水库）, or groundwater（地下水）. Irrigation can dramatically increase crop yields（作物产量）and allow multiple cropping seasons（多季种植）per year, but it requires significant infrastructure investment（基础设施投资）and can deplete water resources（耗尽水资源）, cause soil salinisation（土壤盐渍化）, and damage aquatic ecosystems（水生生态系统）if not managed sustainably.

The global food system（全球食物系统）faces the challenge of feeding a projected population of nearly 10 billion people by 2050 while reducing agriculture's environmental footprint（环境足迹）. This requires increasing food production by approximately 50 to 70 percent above current levels, primarily through yield increases（产量增加）on existing agricultural land rather than through expansion into forests and natural habitats（自然栖息地）. Achieving this increase sustainably — without degrading the soil, depleting water resources, increasing greenhouse gas emissions（温室气体排放）, or destroying biodiversity（破坏生物多样性）— is one of the defining challenges of the twenty-first century.

Land, water, and agricultural production therefore represent the mechanism through which societies use land and water to produce food and how the limits of these resources shape the challenge of feeding a growing population. The vocabulary of agricultural production — agriculture, rain-fed agriculture, irrigated agriculture, arable land, food surplus, global food system — names the resources that societies depend on for food production and the systems through which those resources are managed. Agricultural texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from land and water availability through farming systems to the food production outcomes that determine whether societies can feed their populations sustainably.

## Soil Quality and Crop Growth（土壤质量与作物生长）

Soil quality（土壤质量）is the capacity of soil to support plant growth, maintain environmental health（维护环境健康）, and sustain agricultural productivity over time. Good soil provides physical support for plant roots（植物根系）, holds water and nutrients in forms accessible to plants（以植物可获取的形式保持水分和养分）, allows air to reach roots for respiration（呼吸作用）, and hosts a diverse community of organisms（生物群落）that recycle organic matter（有机质）, suppress disease（抑制病害）, and maintain soil structure. Soil is the foundation of terrestrial food production（陆地食物生产的基础）, and its quality determines how much food can be grown on a given area of land.

Soil is composed of mineral particles（矿物质颗粒）, organic matter（有机质）, water, air, and living organisms in a complex matrix（复杂基质）. The mineral particles come from weathered rock（风化岩石）and are classified by size: sand（沙粒）(largest, 0.05–2 mm), silt（粉粒）(0.002–0.05 mm), and clay（黏粒）(smallest, less than 0.002 mm). The proportion of these particles determines soil texture（土壤质地）, which affects drainage（排水）, water retention（水分保持）, nutrient holding capacity（养分保持能力）, and workability（可耕性）. Sandy soils drain quickly and warm rapidly in spring but hold less water and nutrients. Clay soils hold water and nutrients well but drain slowly, warm slowly, and can become compacted（压实）and waterlogged（积水）. Loam（壤土）— a balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay — provides the optimal combination of drainage, water retention, and nutrient availability for most crops.

Organic matter in soil comes from decomposed plants, animals, and microorganisms. Humus（腐殖质）— the stable end product of decomposition（分解的最终稳定产物）— improves soil structure by binding mineral particles into aggregates（团聚体）, increases water-holding capacity（水分保持能力）, provides a slow-release reservoir（缓释储库）of nutrients, and supports the soil food web（土壤食物网）of bacteria, fungi（真菌）, protozoa（原生动物）, nematodes（线虫）, earthworms（蚯蚓）, and arthropods（节肢动物）that drive nutrient cycling（养分循环）. A single teaspoon of healthy soil contains more microorganisms than there are people on Earth. Soil organic matter can be increased through practices such as adding compost（堆肥）, growing cover crops（覆盖作物）, incorporating crop residues（作物残留物还田）, and reducing tillage（减少耕作）.

Soil fertility（土壤肥力）refers to the ability of soil to provide essential nutrients（必需养分）to plants in adequate quantities and appropriate forms. The most important nutrients for plant growth are nitrogen（氮 / N）, phosphorus（磷 / P）, and potassium（钾 / K）— the primary macronutrients（主要大量营养素）supplied by most fertilisers（化肥）. Plants also require secondary nutrients（次要养分）— calcium（钙）, magnesium（镁）, sulphur（硫）— and micronutrients（微量营养素）— iron（铁）, zinc（锌）, copper（铜）, manganese（锰）, boron（硼）, molybdenum（钼）— in smaller quantities. When crops are harvested, nutrients are removed from the soil and must be replaced through fertiliser application（施肥）, biological nitrogen fixation（生物固氮）, nutrient recycling（养分循环）, or natural weathering processes（自然风化过程）to maintain long-term productivity.

Soil degradation（土壤退化）is the decline in soil quality caused by human activity and natural processes. Erosion（侵蚀）removes topsoil（表土）— the most fertile layer — faster than it can form. Nutrient depletion（养分耗竭）occurs when harvest removals exceed nutrient inputs. Salinisation（盐渍化）accumulates salts in the root zone through irrigation with saline water（含盐水灌溉）or poor drainage. Compaction（压实）reduces pore space（孔隙空间）, restricting root growth and water infiltration（水分渗透）. Pollution（污染）from pesticides（杀虫剂）, heavy metals（重金属）, and industrial waste（工业废物）contaminates soil and harms soil organisms. Globally, approximately one-third of soils are moderately to severely degraded（中度至严重退化）, threatening the productive capacity（生产能力）needed to feed a growing population. Soil conservation practices（土壤保护实践）— including cover cropping, reduced tillage, contour farming（等高耕作）, crop rotation（轮作）, and agroforestry（农林业）— are essential for maintaining long-term agricultural productivity and environmental health.

Soil quality and crop growth therefore represent the mechanism through which soil structure, organic matter, and nutrient availability determine how much food can be grown on a given area of land. The vocabulary of soil — soil quality, soil texture, organic matter, humus, soil fertility, soil degradation, erosion, salinisation, soil conservation — names the properties that determine soil productivity and the practices that protect or degrade those properties. Agricultural texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from soil composition through nutrient cycling to the crop growth outcomes that determine whether land can sustain agricultural production over time or whether soil degradation reduces its productive capacity.

## Crop Yield and Farming Technology（作物产量与农业技术）

Crop yield（作物产量）is the amount of crop produced per unit of land area, usually measured in tonnes per hectare（吨/公顷）or bushels per acre（蒲式耳/英亩）. Higher yields mean more food can be produced from the same amount of land, which is essential for feeding a growing population without converting additional natural habitats into farmland（将更多自然栖息地转化为农田）. Yield is determined by the interaction of genetic potential（遗传潜力）, environmental conditions（环境条件）— soil quality, water availability, temperature, sunlight — and management practices（管理措施）— fertilisation, pest control（害虫控制）, irrigation, planting density（种植密度）, and harvest timing（收获时机）.

The Green Revolution（绿色革命）of the mid-twentieth century dramatically increased crop yields worldwide through a combination of technological innovations（技术创新）. Plant breeders（植物育种家）developed high-yielding varieties（高产品种）of wheat（小麦）, rice（水稻）, and maize（玉米）that responded strongly to fertiliser and irrigation, producing much more grain per plant than traditional varieties（传统品种）. These varieties had shorter stems（更短的茎秆）that prevented lodging（倒伏）under the weight of heavier grain heads（更重的穗头）. The Green Revolution also introduced expanded irrigation（扩大灌溉）, increased fertiliser use（增加化肥使用）, chemical pest control（化学害虫控制）, and mechanisation（机械化）. This transformation prevented widespread famine（大规模饥荒）in Asia and Latin America（拉丁美洲）, saved hundreds of millions of lives, and allowed food production to keep pace with（跟上）rapid population growth.

Farming technology has continued to advance since the Green Revolution, introducing new tools that increase precision, efficiency, and sustainability. Precision agriculture（精准农业）uses GPS（全球定位系统）, satellite imagery（卫星影像）, soil sensors（土壤传感器）, drones（无人机）, and data analytics（数据分析）to apply water, fertiliser, and pesticides exactly where and when they are needed, reducing waste（减少浪费）and environmental impact（环境影响）while maintaining or increasing yields. Variable-rate technology（变量技术）allows farmers to apply different amounts of inputs to different parts of the same field based on soil conditions and crop needs, rather than applying uniform amounts across the entire area.

Genetically modified crops（转基因作物 / GM crops）have been developed with specific traits（特定性状）that address agricultural challenges. Pest-resistant varieties（抗虫品种）— such as Bt cotton（Bt棉花）and Bt maize — produce proteins（蛋白质）toxic to specific insect pests, reducing the need for chemical insecticides（化学杀虫剂）. Herbicide-tolerant varieties（耐除草剂品种）allow farmers to control weeds（杂草）with specific herbicides without damaging the crop. Drought-tolerant varieties（耐旱品种）maintain yields under water stress. Golden Rice（黄金大米）has been engineered to produce beta-carotene（β-胡萝卜素）, addressing vitamin A deficiency（维生素A缺乏症）in developing countries. The adoption and regulation of GM crops remain contested（有争议的）, with debates about environmental risks（环境风险）, corporate control of seed supplies（企业对种子供应的控制）, labelling requirements（标签要求）, and long-term ecological effects（长期生态效应）.

Crop yields cannot increase indefinitely — there are biological limits（生物学极限）to how much grain a plant can produce given the constraints of photosynthesis efficiency（光合效率）, nutrient availability, and water supply. In some of the most productive agricultural regions（最高产的农业地区）, yields of major crops have plateaued（达到平台期）— approaching the theoretical maximum（理论最大值）for current varieties under optimal conditions. In other regions, yields have declined due to soil degradation, water scarcity（水资源短缺）, and climate change（气候变化）. Sustaining and increasing yields in the future requires continued innovation in plant breeding（植物育种创新）, soil management（土壤管理）, water efficiency（用水效率）, and integrated pest management（综合虫害管理）, combined with policies that support smallholder farmers（小农户）who produce much of the food in developing countries.

Crop yield and farming technology therefore represent the mechanism through which technological innovation increases the amount of food that can be produced from a given area of land. The vocabulary of crop yield — crop yield, Green Revolution, high-yielding variety, precision agriculture, genetically modified crop, biological limit — names the technologies that have increased food production and the constraints that limit further increases. Agricultural texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from technological innovation through yield increases to the food production outcomes that determine whether societies can feed growing populations without expanding agricultural land into natural habitats.

## Intensive Farming and Environmental Pressure（密集农业与环境压力）

Intensive farming（密集农业 / 集约化农业）uses large amounts of external inputs（外部投入）— synthetic fertiliser（合成化肥）, chemical pesticides（化学杀虫剂）, irrigation water, energy（能源）, and machinery（机械）— to achieve high yields per unit of land. Intensive farming produces large quantities of food at relatively low cost per unit, feeding billions of people and supporting global food supply chains（全球食物供应链）. This production model（生产模式）has been enormously successful in increasing total food output（总食物产出）, but it creates significant environmental pressure（环境压力）that threatens the long-term sustainability of agricultural systems.

Excess fertiliser（过量化肥）that is not absorbed by crops can run off（径流流失）into rivers, lakes, and coastal waters（沿海水域）or leach（淋溶）into groundwater（地下水）. This nutrient pollution（养分污染）causes eutrophication（富营养化）— a process where excess nitrogen and phosphorus stimulate rapid algal growth（藻类快速生长）in water bodies. When the algae die and decompose（藻类死亡和分解）, the decomposition process consumes dissolved oxygen（溶解氧）, creating hypoxic zones（缺氧区）or "dead zones"（死亡区）where fish and other aquatic organisms cannot survive. The Gulf of Mexico dead zone（墨西哥湾死亡区）, caused primarily by fertiliser runoff from the Mississippi River basin（密西西比河流域）, covers thousands of square kilometres each summer. Fertiliser runoff is also a major source of nitrate contamination（硝酸盐污染）in drinking water, posing health risks to humans, particularly infants（婴儿）.

Pesticides（杀虫剂）— including insecticides（杀虫剂）, herbicides（除草剂）, and fungicides（杀菌剂）— control organisms that damage crops, reducing yield losses and improving food quality. However, pesticides can also harm beneficial insects（有益昆虫）such as bees（蜜蜂）and other pollinators（传粉者）that are essential for the reproduction of many crops and wild plants. Pesticide residues（农药残留）can contaminate water sources（水源）, accumulate in food chains（在食物链中积累）, and affect human health through occupational exposure（职业暴露）among farm workers（农业工人）and dietary exposure（膳食暴露）among consumers. The development of pesticide resistance（杀虫剂耐药性）in pest populations is an ongoing evolutionary arms race（进化军备竞赛）— as pests evolve resistance to existing chemicals, new pesticides must be developed, creating a cycle of escalating chemical use（不断升级的化学品使用循环）.

Intensive livestock farming（集约化畜牧业）— raising large numbers of animals in confined animal feeding operations（集中动物饲养场 / CAFOs）— produces meat（肉类）, eggs（蛋类）, and dairy products（乳制品）efficiently and at scale. This system concentrates animal waste（动物粪便）in quantities that exceed the capacity of surrounding land to absorb it as fertiliser, creating water pollution（水污染）and air pollution（空气污染）from ammonia（氨气）, hydrogen sulphide（硫化氢）, and methane（甲烷）. Livestock farming is a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions（温室气体排放）, particularly methane from enteric fermentation（肠道发酵）in cattle（牛）and nitrous oxide（氧化亚氮）from manure management（粪便管理）. The global livestock sector（畜牧业部门）accounts for approximately 14.5 percent of all anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions（人为温室气体排放）.

The environmental pressure from intensive farming has driven growing interest in alternative approaches that maintain productivity while reducing ecological harm. Integrated nutrient management（综合养分管理）optimises fertiliser use by matching applications to crop needs and soil conditions. Integrated pest management（综合虫害管理）combines biological control（生物防治）, cultural practices（栽培措施）, and targeted chemical use to control pests with minimal environmental impact. Conservation agriculture（保护性农业）minimises soil disturbance, maintains permanent soil cover, and diversifies crop rotations to protect soil health. These approaches represent a shift toward farming systems that work with ecological processes（与生态过程协同）rather than against them.

Intensive farming and environmental pressure therefore represent the mechanism through which high-input agriculture increases food production while creating environmental costs that threaten long-term sustainability. The vocabulary of intensive farming — intensive farming, nutrient pollution, eutrophication, pesticide resistance, confined animal feeding operation, integrated pest management, conservation agriculture — names the practices that increase agricultural output and the environmental consequences that arise from those practices. Agricultural texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from input use through environmental impact to the sustainability outcomes that determine whether farming systems can maintain productivity over time or whether environmental degradation reduces their long-term capacity.

## Organic Farming and Sustainable Agriculture（有机农业与可持续农业）

Organic farming（有机农业）avoids synthetic fertilisers（合成化肥）, synthetic pesticides（合成农药）, genetically modified organisms（转基因生物）, and growth hormones（生长激素）. Organic farmers use natural methods to maintain soil fertility and control pests: crop rotation（轮作）alternates crops to break pest cycles（打破害虫周期）and maintain nutrient balance; compost（堆肥）and green manure（绿肥）build soil organic matter; biological pest control（生物害虫防治）uses natural predators（天敌）and beneficial organisms; and mechanical cultivation（机械耕作）controls weeds without herbicides（不使用除草剂）.

Organic farming supports higher on-farm biodiversity（更高的农场内生物多样性）because it avoids broad-spectrum pesticides（广谱杀虫剂）that harm beneficial insects and other wildlife. Organic practices build soil organic matter, improving soil structure, water retention, and biological activity. Organic farming avoids the energy-intensive production（能源密集型生产）of synthetic nitrogen fertiliser, which requires large amounts of natural gas（天然气）as both feedstock and fuel. Organic farms typically have lower nutrient runoff（更低的养分径流）, reduced pesticide contamination（更少的农药污染）, and higher populations of pollinators（更多的传粉者种群）compared with conventional farms（常规农场）of similar size.

Organic farming generally produces lower yields（更低的产量）than intensive conventional farming（集约化常规农业）, particularly for staple cereal crops（主要谷类作物）in high-productivity regions. Yield gaps（产量差距）vary by crop, region, and management quality — they are smaller for perennial crops（多年生作物）, legumes（豆类）, and in developing countries where conventional input use is already low. The lower yield means that organic farming requires more land to produce the same amount of food. If all global agriculture were converted to organic methods without other changes, more natural habitats would need to be converted to farmland to maintain current food production levels — a trade-off（权衡）between reduced chemical use and increased land use that has important environmental implications（环境影响）.

Sustainable agriculture（可持续农业）is a broader concept than organic farming. It aims to produce food in ways that are environmentally sound（环境友好的）, economically viable（经济可行的）, and socially responsible（社会负责的）— meeting current food needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Sustainable agriculture is defined by its outcomes（结果）rather than by specific prohibited inputs（特定禁止投入）, and it encompasses a range of practices and systems.

Practices that contribute to sustainable agriculture include multiple approaches that work together. Crop rotation（轮作）grows different crops in sequence on the same land to maintain soil fertility, break pest and disease cycles, and reduce the need for chemical inputs. Cover cropping（覆盖种植）plants crops specifically to protect and enrich the soil between main crop seasons, preventing erosion, suppressing weeds, and adding organic matter. Conservation tillage（保护性耕作）reduces or eliminates ploughing（犁地）to protect soil structure, maintain soil cover, reduce erosion, and preserve soil moisture（保持土壤水分）. Integrated pest management（综合虫害管理）uses a combination of biological, cultural, and chemical methods to control pests with minimal environmental impact, applying chemicals only when necessary and choosing the least harmful options. Agroforestry（农林业）integrates trees with crops or livestock, improving soil health, providing shade and windbreaks（防风林）, sequestering carbon（固碳）, and diversifying farm income（多样化农场收入）.

Organic farming and sustainable agriculture therefore represent the mechanism through which farming systems attempt to maintain productivity while reducing environmental harm. The vocabulary of sustainable agriculture — organic farming, sustainable agriculture, yield gap, crop rotation, cover cropping, conservation tillage, agroforestry — names the practices that reduce chemical inputs and protect soil health and the trade-offs that arise when farming systems prioritise environmental sustainability over maximum yield. Agricultural texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from farming practice through environmental impact to the sustainability outcomes that determine whether agricultural systems can meet current food needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

## Supply Chains and Food Distribution（供应链与食物分配）

A food supply chain（食物供应链）is the network of organisations, people, activities, information, and resources involved in moving food from producer to consumer（从生产者到消费者）. The chain includes farmers（农民）, input suppliers（投入品供应商）, processors（加工商）, distributors（分销商）, wholesalers（批发商）, retailers（零售商）, and consumers（消费者）. Each stage adds value（增加价值）, transforms the product, and moves it closer to the final consumer, but each stage also introduces costs, potential losses, and environmental impacts.

Food supply chains have become increasingly global（全球化）. A product grown in one country may be processed in a second, packaged in a third, and sold in a fourth. This global food system（全球食物系统）allows consumers to access a wide variety of foods year-round（全年获取各种食物）, regardless of local growing seasons（当地生长季节）. It allows countries to specialise in producing foods for which they have a comparative advantage（比较优势）— tropical fruits（热带水果）from equatorial regions（赤道地区）, grains（谷物）from temperate plains（温带平原）, seafood（海鲜）from coastal nations（沿海国家）. Global trade（全球贸易）also provides food security benefits by allowing food-deficit regions（食物短缺地区）to import from surplus regions（盈余地区）, buffering against local crop failures（本地作物歉收）.

Long and complex supply chains create vulnerabilities（脆弱性）that can disrupt food availability and prices. Disruptions at any point — a crop failure（作物歉收）in a major exporting country（主要出口国）, a transport strike（运输罢工）, a trade dispute（贸易争端）, a pandemic（大流行病）, or a geopolitical conflict（地缘政治冲突）— can affect food availability and prices worldwide. The COVID-19 pandemic revealed how fragile some food supply chains can be when transport is disrupted, labour is unavailable, and borders close（边境关闭）. The Russia-Ukraine conflict（俄乌冲突）disrupted global wheat and fertiliser supplies, causing food price spikes（食品价格飙升）that affected millions of people in import-dependent countries（依赖进口的国家）.

Food distribution（食物分配）refers to how food reaches consumers and whether all people have physical and economic access to adequate nutrition（充足营养）. Even when enough food is produced globally — current global production is sufficient to feed the entire population — it may not reach everyone who needs it. Poor infrastructure（基础设施差）, lack of market access（市场可及性不足）, poverty（贫困）, conflict（冲突）, and political instability（政治不稳定）can prevent food from reaching people in remote or disadvantaged areas. Food is distributed according to purchasing power（购买力）rather than need, which means that hunger（饥饿）persists alongside abundance（丰富）.

Approximately one-third of all food produced globally for human consumption — about 1.3 billion tonnes per year — is lost or wasted（损失或浪费）somewhere along the supply chain. In developing countries, most food loss（食物损失）happens early in the supply chain due to poor harvesting techniques（收获技术差）, inadequate storage（储存不足）, lack of refrigeration（缺乏冷藏）, and inefficient transport（低效运输）. In developed countries, most food waste（食物浪费）happens at the retail and consumer level（零售和消费环节）when food is discarded uneaten（被丢弃未食用）— driven by over-purchasing（过度购买）, confusion about date labels（日期标签混淆）, large portion sizes（大份量）, and aesthetic standards（外观标准）that reject imperfect produce（不完美的农产品）. Reducing food loss and waste is one of the most effective strategies for improving food security and reducing agriculture's environmental footprint.

Supply chains and food distribution therefore represent the mechanism through which food moves from producers to consumers and how disruptions in that movement affect food availability and prices. The vocabulary of supply chains — food supply chain, global food system, food distribution, food loss, food waste, cold chain infrastructure — names the stages through which food travels and the vulnerabilities that can disrupt that travel. Agricultural texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from farm production through supply chain stages to the distribution outcomes that determine whether food reaches all consumers or whether supply chain disruptions and food waste leave millions without adequate nutrition.

## Food Security and Climate Risk（粮食安全与气候风险）

Food security（粮食安全）exists when all people, at all times, have physical, social, and economic access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food that meets their dietary needs and food preferences for an active and healthy life. Food security has four interconnected dimensions（四个相互关联的维度）: availability（可获得性）— enough food is produced or imported to meet the population's needs; access（可及性）— people can afford and physically reach food; utilisation（利用）— people can prepare, store, and consume food safely and absorb its nutrients; and stability（稳定性）— food security is not threatened by sudden shocks（突发冲击）such as drought, conflict, or price spikes.

Climate change（气候变化）is a major and growing threat to food security across all four dimensions. Higher temperatures reduce yields（产量）of major staple crops（主要粮食作物）— wheat, maize, rice, and soybean（大豆）— in many regions, particularly in tropical and subtropical areas（热带和亚热带地区）where temperatures already approach crop tolerance limits（作物耐受极限）. Changing rainfall patterns（降雨模式变化）make farming more unpredictable — some regions experience more frequent droughts（更频繁的干旱）, others more intense rainfall and flooding（更强烈的降雨和洪水）. More frequent extreme weather events（更频繁的极端天气事件）— heatwaves（热浪）, droughts, floods, storms — can destroy crops, damage infrastructure, disrupt supply chains, and cause sudden food price increases（食品价格突然上涨）. Rising CO₂ levels can stimulate plant growth（刺激植物生长）through the CO₂ fertilisation effect（二氧化碳施肥效应）, but this benefit is often offset（被抵消）by concurrent heat stress（同时发生的热胁迫）, water limitations, nutrient constraints, and increased pest pressure（增加的害虫压力）.

The regions most vulnerable to climate-related food insecurity（气候相关粮食不安全）are often those that already struggle with hunger and poverty — sub-Saharan Africa（撒哈拉以南非洲）, South Asia（南亚）, and parts of Central America（中美洲部分地区）. These regions are disproportionately located in tropical and subtropical areas where temperatures are already high and rainfall is variable. Smallholder farmers（小农户）who depend on rain-fed agriculture（依赖雨养农业）are especially vulnerable because they have limited resources to invest in irrigation, drought-tolerant varieties（耐旱品种）, or crop insurance（作物保险）. Climate change therefore threatens to widen existing inequalities（加大现有不平等）in food access between wealthy and poor regions.

Adapting agriculture to climate change（农业适应气候变化）requires multiple strategies operating at different scales. Developing crop varieties（开发作物品种）that are more tolerant of heat（耐热）, drought（耐旱）, flooding（耐涝）, and salinity（耐盐）through conventional breeding（常规育种）and genetic technologies（基因技术）provides biological tools for adaptation. Improving water management（改善水资源管理）through more efficient irrigation（更高效的灌溉）, water storage（蓄水）, rainwater harvesting（雨水收集）, and soil moisture conservation（土壤水分保持）reduces vulnerability to rainfall variability（降雨变率）. Diversifying crops（多样化种植）and livelihoods（生计多样化）spreads risk across multiple sources of income. Improving early warning systems（早期预警系统）for extreme weather and food shortages allows governments and communities to prepare and respond before crises develop.

Achieving global food security in a changing climate requires increasing food production, reducing poverty and inequality, improving market access（改善市场可及性）, reducing food waste, building more resilient food systems（建设更具韧性的食物系统）, and addressing the root causes of climate change through mitigation（减缓）. Food security connects agriculture with economic development（经济发展）, social policy（社会政策）, environmental sustainability（环境可持续性）, and climate action（气候行动）, making it one of the most complex and urgent challenges facing humanity.

Food security and climate risk therefore represent the mechanism through which climate change threatens the ability of all people to access sufficient, safe, and nutritious food. The vocabulary of food security — food security, availability, access, utilisation, stability, climate-related food insecurity, smallholder farmer — names the dimensions through which food security is achieved and the climate threats that can disrupt those dimensions. Agricultural texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from climate change through crop yield impacts to the food security outcomes that determine whether populations can maintain adequate nutrition or whether climate-driven crop failures push millions into hunger.

## Food Waste and Resource Use（食物浪费与资源使用）

Food waste（食物浪费）occurs at every stage of the food supply chain（食物供应链的每个环节）, from production on the farm to consumption at the table. The scale of food waste represents an enormous inefficiency（低效）in the global food system — resources are used to produce food that is never consumed, while hundreds of millions of people remain food-insecure（粮食不安全的）.

Roughly one-third of all food produced for human consumption is lost or wasted annually. This represents wasted land（被浪费的土地）, water（水）, energy（能源）, labour（劳动）, fertiliser（化肥）, and other inputs that went into producing food that was never eaten. The land area used to grow food that is ultimately wasted is larger than the total agricultural land of any single country except China and India. Food waste also generates greenhouse gas emissions（温室气体排放）when it decomposes（分解）in landfills（垃圾填埋场）, producing methane（甲烷）— a greenhouse gas approximately 25 times more potent than CO₂ over a 100-year period. If global food waste were a country, it would be the third largest emitter of greenhouse gases（第三大温室气体排放国）after China and the United States.

Reducing food waste requires action at multiple levels of the supply chain, tailored to the specific causes of waste at each stage. At the production level（生产环节）, improved harvesting techniques（改进收获技术）, better on-farm storage（更好的农场储存）, and access to markets（市场可及性）can reduce losses in developing countries. At the processing and distribution level（加工和分销环节）, improved cold chain infrastructure（冷链基础设施）— refrigerated transport（冷藏运输）and storage — prevents spoilage（腐败）of perishable foods（易腐食品）. At the retail level（零售环节）, better inventory management（库存管理）, dynamic pricing（动态定价）for products approaching their sell-by date（销售截止日期）, and donation of unsold food（未售出食物的捐赠）to food banks（食物银行）can reduce waste. At the consumer level（消费环节）, better meal planning（更好的膳食计划）, proper food storage（适当的食物储存）, understanding of date labels（理解日期标签）— distinguishing "best before"（最佳食用日期）from "use by"（使用截止日期）— and creative use of leftovers（剩余食物的创造性使用）can reduce household waste.

Some food waste is unavoidable（不可避免的）— peels（果皮）, bones（骨头）, shells（壳）, and other inedible parts（不可食用部分）of food cannot be consumed directly. This organic waste（有机废物）can be composted（堆肥）to return nutrients to the soil, creating a circular system（循环系统）where food waste becomes a resource for future food production. Composting（堆肥）converts organic waste into nutrient-rich soil amendment（富含养分的土壤改良剂）, closing the nutrient loop（闭合养分循环）and reducing dependence on synthetic fertilisers. Anaerobic digestion（厌氧消化）can convert food waste into biogas（沼气）for energy production and digestate（消化液）for fertiliser, extracting additional value before the nutrients return to the soil.

Food waste and resource use therefore represent the mechanism through which food that is produced but never consumed represents a waste of land, water, energy, and labour while generating greenhouse gas emissions. The vocabulary of food waste — food waste, food loss, cold chain infrastructure, composting, anaerobic digestion, circular system — names the stages at which food is wasted and the strategies that can reduce that waste. Agricultural texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from food production through supply chain stages to the waste outcomes that determine whether food reaches consumers or whether it is lost along the way, and how reducing food waste can improve food security while reducing agriculture's environmental footprint.
